new_en: (43) "Where all are kohanim," etc. This applies specifically when there is no Levi there at all, so that the order established by the Sages cannot be followed, and therefore it is preferable to alter the order for the sake of peace. But if there is even 1 Levi there, they read in the order stated in the Mishnah: Kohen, Levi, Yisrael, and afterward the remaining aliyot are given to kohanim. (44) "One Yisrael among them." If there are 2 Yisraelim, and all the more so if there are more, this falls under what the Shulchan Aruch writes afterward, that there are not enough Yisraelim to fill all the aliyot. Therefore a kohen reads first, a kohen also reads in place of the Levi, then the Yisraelim read, and the remaining aliyot are completed by kohanim. If there are 2 Levites and 2 Yisraelim, the order is Kohen, Levi, Yisrael, then another Kohen, Levi, Yisrael, and a kohen reads seventh, and certainly the same applies to additional aliyot. (45) "For the sake of peace." So that each one should not say, "Why are you called first rather than I?" The same applies when there is only 1 Levi in a city consisting entirely of kohanim: that Levi reads first for this reason. If there are only kohanim and Levites, a kohen may read after a kohen when a Levi intervenes between them. A kohen who is a mourner, when there is no other kohen in the synagogue on Shabbos, may be called as Kohen so that public mourning will not be apparent. On a weekday he should not receive the aliyah, because a mourner is forbidden Torah study. Nevertheless, both on a weekday and on Shabbos it is preferable that he leave the synagogue before the reading begins, and they should call a Yisrael and a Levi in place of a kohen. [Eliyah Rabbah and other authorities]

[1] After Torah scholars come the sons of Torah scholars whose fathers are appointed over the community, and after them the communal leaders. This is the order stated by the Tur. Levush writes that in places where mitzvah honors are sold, the purchaser may call whomever he wishes, but each person should nevertheless be called according to his honor. Shach, Choshen Mishpat siman 382, cites Maharshal, Perek HaChovel, siman 60, that if one purchased the third, sixth, or seventh aliyah and another person preempted him, the latter is liable for 10 gold coins if the purchaser seized them; Shach writes that this is not compelling. Shiyarei Knesset HaGedolah did not see the words of Shach. Maharshal discusses a case where Reuven was called to the Torah and Shimon preempted him and recited the blessings. He is liable only if Reuven was unable to answer Amen to Shimon's blessing or to recite the blessing quietly for himself. If he could answer Amen, Shimon is exempt. It appears that where liability applies, it is 10 gold coins for each blessing, thus 20 in all, as Perishah writes in Yoreh De'ah siman 28. There is therefore no need to alter Maharshal's text. Responsa Nachalat Shivah, siman 38, did not see these sources, and the proof it brings from Tosafos, Chullin 87a, requires consideration.

Where several bridegrooms are present and all are Yisraelim, precedence is given, when their Torah standing is equal, in the following order: one marrying a virgin, then one marrying a widow, then one marrying a chalutzah, then one marrying a divorcee. See siman 282 regarding other rules of precedence among those obligated to receive an aliyah. The enactments attributed to Maharal of Prague list among those with a special claim: a bridegroom on the wedding day or on the Shabbos following the wedding, a bar mitzvah boy, the 2 shoshvinim, a sandak, a mohel, the husband of a woman who gave birth, and one observing a yahrzeit. The status of the shoshvinim after the wedding requires consideration, since Levush in siman 282 does not mention it.

Magen Avraham writes that if a woman who gave birth is ill and cannot come to the synagogue, her husband has no special obligation to receive an aliyah until she comes. At 40 days after the birth of a male, or 80 days after the birth of a female, he has an obligation because of the offering associated with childbirth. If his wife died, he has no such obligation. A husband whose wife miscarried has a claim unless there is uncertainty whether a recognizable fetal form had developed.

Nachalat Tzvi, siman 38, writes that a yahrzeit takes precedence over a communal leader, and that one may take steps to preserve this right because once the day passes the opportunity cannot be recovered. Shiyarei Knesset HaGedolah records the following order in cases of competing honors connected with Sifrei Torah and communal mitzvot: a bridegroom precedes one holding the lighting honor; the father of a newborn precedes the bridegroom; a baal brit precedes the father of the newborn. Where 2 fathers, 2 baalei brit, or 2 bridegrooms are otherwise equal, a Torah scholar who is a halachic decisor precedes a Torah scholar who is sharp but is not a decisor; a Torah scholar precedes an unlearned kohen; a kohen precedes a Levi; and a Levi precedes a Yisrael. Between 2 fathers of equal standing, the one whose child was born first takes precedence, since his mitzvah came first. The custom of that city was likewise that the child born first receives the brit milah first. Between equal bridegrooms, equal holders of the lighting honor, or fathers whose children were born at the same time, they cast lots. One whose Sefer Torah he personally purchased and had written precedes one who inherited a Sefer Torah. One whose Sefer Torah is regularly in that congregation precedes one whose Sefer Torah is elsewhere and who wishes to bring it there for that Shabbos. Levush's statement that each person should be called according to his honor strongly supports these rules, as Lechem Rav concludes, and Responsa Maharam Mintz, siman 6, implies likewise. If a gabbai refuses to call a Torah scholar out of spite, the communal officers should enact a regulation and remove him from his position.

Seif katan 1, "and one reads," etc. "So as not to shame the first and the last" is the text in Bach in the name of Maharshal, although Bach questioned its source. It appears that Maharshal said this as a matter of reasoning. If the chazzan reads 4 verses for the first or the last reader, there is no embarrassment to the others, because everyone knows that the first aliyah possesses importance by virtue of being first, as Magen Avraham writes in the following seif katan. Thus, reading 4 verses for the first is understood as honor for the aliyah itself, not personal honor for the reader. The same is true of the last aliyah, whose distinction is also generally known. The distinction of the middle reader, however, which Magen Avraham relates to the arrangement of the menorah, is not as widely known. People may therefore suspect that the chazzan gave the second reader 4 verses because of that reader's personal honor, which could embarrass the others. In Talmudic times, when the oleh himself read, this concern did not arise in the same way: if the second reader chose to read 4 verses, the last reader was not embarrassed merely because the second person honored himself by reading more.

Seif 10, "after," etc. This is analogous to Birkat HaMazon, where one returns to the place at which he stopped. Rif and the other authorities explain that he returns and says, "Blessed is the One from Whose food we have eaten," etc. "In order to include," etc. Although he says "HaMevorach," the law differs from Birkat HaMazon, where the leader says "Nevarech" in order to include himself and then repeats "Baruch." The reason is that "Barechu" is an expression of praise rather than a request, unlike expressions such as "Give greatness" or "Say to God," as appears from the Yerushalmi and Bereishit Rabbah.

The blessings over the Torah are treated like the blessings over other mitzvot. The Yerushalmi, Berachos chapter 7, discusses the enactment that each reader recites a blessing. Before that enactment, the first reader would bless before the reading and the last after it. The same principle appears in the Tosefta concerning a synagogue in which no one is able to read, and see the end of siman 143. See also Tosafos, Rosh Hashana 33a.

Seif 9, "that it is no worse," etc., follows the principle stated in the first chapter of Berachos. Seif 10, "the final blessing," is based on the Mishnah and Gemara at the beginning of the third chapter of Megillah, Berachos 21a, Masekhet Soferim 13:8, and the Yerushalmi, Berachos chapter 7. The Yerushalmi asks how the blessing over Torah reading applies when an individual reads alone, since the source from zimun concerns a group. It answers that the Sages treated Torah reading like the other mitzvot of the Torah, each of which has its blessing. This is also the basis of the ruling in siman 692, seif 1, in the Rama.

"This is the Written Torah," as it is written, "and that which was written was upright, words of truth." "And life," etc., is connected to the conclusion of the verse concerning "the words of the wise." In the first chapter of Chagigah they expounded that just as a goad directs the animal, words of Torah direct a person and impart life. The continuation, "like nails firmly planted," refers to the Oral Torah, as indicated by "the words of the wise" and "masters of assemblies"; the Sages expounded that these declare one matter pure and those declare it impure, yet all are words of Torah.

"One should not build," etc. It appears that this applies specifically in a city whose inhabitants are all Jews. Nowadays in our exile, when we live as a small minority among non-Jews and they become jealous of us if we build tall structures, it is preferable to apply to ourselves, "Why should you make yourself conspicuous?" and to lower our houses further, thereby satisfying all views, both before Heaven and before people. [Bach] For us, the entrance should be made on the west, and likewise toward the north and south. [Hagahot Maimoniyot, chapter 11 of Hilchot Tefillah]

There, "fit to place." Meaning: regarding ritual impurity, the reason a broken earthenware shard can contract impurity is that it is fit to be placed beneath dripping liquid. Therefore its minimum useful size is determined by a hole through which liquid can escape, because one does not place one broken shard beneath another broken shard. Washing the hands is different. The reason a broken vessel is valid for washing is not that it can be placed beneath drips, but because the Sages did not require specifically an intact vessel for washing. They required only that it be capable of holding a revi'it, even if it is a broken vessel. Thus, for this law an intact vessel and a broken vessel are equivalent, and the disqualifying size of the hole is one through which liquid can enter.

One who washes his hands pours some of the revi'it over them to remove dirt and anything that intervenes, then pours a second time. These waters are also impure. He then pours a third time in order to purify the water remaining on the hands. If there is no dirt or intervening substance on his hands, he pours a full revi'it over both hands at once and does not need second waters. {Rama: The same applies if he has abundant water. He first washes with a small amount to remove the dirt, then pours a revi'it at once, and does not need a third pouring. One who washes his hands must rub them together. [Rambam, chapter 11 of Hilchot Mikvaot; Kol Bo; Semag; Rosh, chapter Kol HaBasar]}

"Upon them." See Taz and Magen Avraham for the reason. "For all of this." If another person whose hands are impure touched them, see Magen Avraham. A vessel with a hole in its bottom in which a stopper is inserted, and the stopper is pushed upward so that the water flows out, may be used. Although the stopper is moist and he touches it with his hands, there is no concern. Lechem Chamudot. Magen Avraham writes that one should nevertheless be concerned that after washing the first hand, when he again pushes the stopper with that wet hand, some of the impure water adheres to the stopper. When he then pushes it with the second hand, that hand can become impure from the moisture. He should therefore pour a revi'it at once. Likewise, if he grasps the vessel with his wet hand, the handle becomes impure from the water. If he then grasps it again with the first hand, that hand becomes impure from it and must be dried, as stated in seif 4. Therefore he should pour a revi'it at once. It is also effective to pour first and second waters separately over each hand. See Magen Avraham.
